summary: The paper proposes LayerBudget, a greedy marginal-gain allocator that assigns each transformer layer a token-retention count n_l and a KV bit-width b_l under a global memory budget, plus two auxiliary tricks (an 'inverted' early-layer importance prior and mean-fill for evicted positions). The empirical sweep is unusually broad for this area (7 models 7B-72B, 17 reimplemented baselines, 8 task families, 16K-32K context, a 72B run). My problem is that the paper's own tables do not support its headline claims. On the metric the paper leads with (WikiText-2 PPL ratio), the 2024 pure-quantization baseline KIVI ties or beats LayerBudget at 4x on every model in Table 2 and beats it decisively at 6x on all seven models; in the paper's only memory-vs-quality table, LayerBudget consumes MORE memory (12,939 KB vs 9,990 KB) and delivers WORSE PPL (1.07 vs 1.01) than KIVI at the same nominal 6x. The paper's own component ablation (A1) shows the joint allocator is dominated by both of its constituent parts (Mistral 6x: joint 3.23 vs quant-only 1.00 vs eviction-only 3.18; Llama-2 6x: 45.09 vs 1.01 vs 44.71), the precision-level ablation (A3) shows the INT8 level contributes exactly zero, and the budget sweep concedes that below 3.5x 'no tokens are evicted and Gini has no effect' -- i.e. in the regime where the method is near-lossless it degenerates to uniform INT4 (= KIVI), and in the regime where allocation actually matters it loses. The escape hatch is a carved-out ranking ('first among token-compression methods') that excludes exactly the method that wins, and a retrieval argument resting on NIAH cells of n=15 questions where a '93.3% vs 100%' gap is one question. Several abstract/intro sentences are directly falsified by the paper's own tables. Combined with a memory-accounting inconsistency of 2x between two architecturally identical models, an unverified baseline suite that puts SnapKV below chance on MMLU, a motivating figure that is wrong by ~16x, and LaTeX that does not compile as submitted, I cannot recommend acceptance.
strengths: The experimental surface is genuinely larger than most submissions in this area: seven models spanning MHA and GQA from 7B to 72B, two GPU classes, 17 baselines behind a unified interface, and eight evaluation settings (WikiText-2 PPL, MMLU, GSM8K, NIAH, RULER, LongBench, TPOT, memory). The 32K-context and Qwen2.5-72B runs are real engineering effort that many competing papers skip.

The paper reports the numbers needed to audit it. The component ablation (Table A1), the precision-level ablation (A3), the zero-fill table, the allocator-vs-runtime byte reconciliation, the per-model F(b) calibration table, and the LB-KV NIAH result are all present with raw values. Many submissions would have omitted the tables that let a reviewer check the headline claims; this one does not, and that made a substantive review possible.

Mean-fill is a simple, cheap, and clearly-measured intervention with a large effect that is isolated properly: logits KL 0.249 -> 0.009 on Mistral-7B at 6x, 0.6696 -> 0.0636 on Llama-2-7B, PPL ratio 45.09 -> 1.13, plus median-fill and matched-moment random-fill controls confirming that preserving the first moment is what matters. This is the one component whose isolating experiment shows a large, reproducible marginal effect.

The paper attempts head-to-head comparisons against the closest concurrent work (MoE-nD) and against an orthogonal axis (xKV cross-layer SVD) rather than merely citing them, and it states explicitly that these rows are re-implementations. The comparison design (same WikiText-2 chunks, same memory denominator, same mean-fill) is the right instinct even though the resulting numbers are self-produced.

The Gini-based coverage law C = (n/S)^(1-g) is an elegant O(S)-per-layer signal (last attention row only, not the full S x S matrix), and the paper does at least validate it once against measured attention mass (MAE 3.1% on Mistral-7B) rather than asserting it.
weaknesses: [FATAL, gate (a)] The method loses to or ties the fairest strongest baseline on the metric that matters. In Table 2, KIVI is flat at 1.01-1.02 across all CRs on all four models, while LayerBudget is 1.02/1.03/1.02/1.01 at 4x and 1.17/1.25/1.08/1.03 at 6x -- KIVI ties at 4x and wins on every model at 6x. In Table 1 (the head-to-head), KIVI at 1.006 beats LayerBudget (1.020 / 1.250 on Mistral at 4x/6x; 1.021 / 1.099 on Llama-2-7B) AND beats LayerBudget-KV (1.036 / 1.026) at every single cell -- the paper's own flagship table is won outright by a 2024 baseline, and the caption does not mention it. At 13B-72B the same holds (Llama-2-13B 4x: LB 1.11 vs KIVI 1.02; 72B 6x: LB 1.06 vs KIVI 1.00). Most damningly, the memory-vs-quality table at nominal 6x on Mistral-7B shows LayerBudget at 12,939 KB / 1.07 versus KIVI at 9,990 KB / 1.01: more memory AND worse quality simultaneously. The paper's defense -- 'quantization alone is competitive on PPL but not on retrieval' -- is contradicted by its own NIAH tables, where KIVI ties LayerBudget at 4x on Llama-3.1-8B (100/100), Mistral-7B (73.3/73.3), Qwen3-8B (100/100), Llama-2-13B (100/100), Qwen2.5-14B (100/100), and Qwen2.5-72B (100/100 NIAH, 100/100 RULER at 4x). The entire retrieval argument rests on one model (Llama-2-7B, 93.3 vs 100) at n=15 questions -- literally one question. This is not closable by rewriting; it needs a new experiment showing a regime where LayerBudget beats KIVI at matched bytes on a metric with statistical power.

[FATAL, gate (a)/P12] The paper's central contribution has zero or negative measured marginal effect in its own ablations. Component analysis (A1): at 3x, joint = quant-only = eviction-only (1.00/1.00/1.00 Mistral; 1.02/1.02/1.00 Llama-2, where eviction-only actually WINS); at 6x, joint is worse than BOTH parts (Mistral 3.23 vs quant 1.00 and evict 3.18; Llama-2 45.09 vs 1.01 and 44.71). Precision-level ablation (A3): {4,16} and {4,8,16} are identical at 3 of 4 cells and differ by 0.01 at the fourth -- the INT8 level, one third of the claimed action space, contributes nothing measurable. Budget sweep: 1.5x/2x/3x are explicit ties ('All signal variants are equivalent... no tokens are evicted, and Gini has no effect'). Taken together the paper demonstrates that below ~3.5x LayerBudget degenerates to uniform INT4 (which is KIVI) and above 4x it is dominated. Fix: either produce an experiment in which per-layer joint allocation beats uniform INT4 at matched bytes, or demote the joint allocator from the headline contribution.

Multiple headline claims are directly falsified by the paper's own tables. (i) Abstract: 'achieves PPL ratio <=1.03 at 4x on seven models from 7B to 72B' -- Llama-2-13B is 1.11 at 4x in the large-model scaling table. (ii) Section Analysis: 'at CR=4x and 4096 tokens, LayerBudget matches Full KV accuracy on every model (100%...)' -- the NIAH table shows Mistral-7B LB at 4x = 73.3 against Full KV 86.7. (iii) 'LayerBudget ranks 1st among all token-compression methods... At every configuration across all four models in Table 2' -- MiniKV (a fixed-pyramid eviction + 2-bit method, i.e. a token-compression method) beats LB on Llama-3.1-8B at 6x (1.07 vs 1.08). (iv) Contribution 5 claims '<=1.009' at 16K-32K, but Llama-3.1-8B is 1.035 at 4x at both 16K and 32K. (v) The same bullet claims LB 'outperforms H2O, CAKE, SnapKV, D2O, and Ada-KV' in Table 2, but CAKE, D2O, and Ada-KV do not appear in Table 2 at all. Each of these needs to be corrected in the text, not defended.

The abstract claims LayerBudget 'ranks first among token-compression methods at 2-4x at memory-matched comparison', and Section 'CR definition' promises 'we report a memory-matched comparison in Appendix [REF]' -- but no memory-matched table exists anywhere in the paper. The only memory-vs-quality table is at 6x and shows LayerBudget losing to KIVI on both axes. Similarly, the A1 caption asserts 'Under a memory-matched comparison (Appendix [REF]), quant-only at ~6x requires evicting tokens beyond the INT4 floor and degrades comparably' with no numbers anywhere. The single most load-bearing comparison in the abstract has no supporting evidence in the submission.

The memory accounting is internally inconsistent, and the paper's own reconciliation claim is false by its own tables. Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B have identical KV geometry (32 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128), so their FP16 base KV at a given S must be identical -- yet the memory-savings table reports 189/379/1513 MB for Llama-3.1-8B and 95/191/762 MB for Mistral-7B at S=512/1024/4096, exactly a factor of 2 apart, and reports savings of 71.2% vs 42.9% for the same method at the same nominal CR=2x. (By the paper's own formula M = 2*L*S*H*d*b/8, both should be ~67 MB at S=512, so neither number is right.) Worse, the Byte-CR Reconciliation appendix asserts that 'every method's effective CR ... matches its nominal CR within +/-0.05' across 1,779 checkpoints, but the same savings table reports 24.3% savings on Llama-2-7B at nominal 2x (effective CR 1.32, off by 0.68 = 13x the claimed bound) and 71.2% on Llama-3.1-8B (effective CR 3.47, off by 1.47). Please recompute every memory number from a single, stated accounting and reissue the tables before submitting anywhere.

Fill-mode asymmetry is unresolved and could account for the paper's most dramatic result. Table 2 is captioned 'with inverted importance and mean-fill', but it is never stated whether H2O/SnapKV/StreamingLLM/MiniKV in that table also received mean-fill. The paper's own data shows fill mode moves Llama-2-7B at 6x from 45.09 to 1.13 -- a ~40x swing, the same order of magnitude as the abstract's 'H2O at 4x collapses (83x PPL)'. If LayerBudget is mean-filled and H2O is zero-filled, the abstract's headline contrast is an artifact of the fill mode, not the allocator. Compounding this, Section 'End-to-End Validation' calls zero-fill 'the practical deployment setting', which means the abstract's headline numbers are produced under an evaluation mode the paper itself says is not deployment; the deployment numbers are 1.17 at 4x on Llama-2-7B and 3.23/45.09 at 6x.

The evidence has almost no statistical power at the resolution at which conclusions are drawn. Setup states 6 chunks with cross-chunk PPL std ~2.3, yet the paper distinguishes 1.000 vs 1.006 vs 1.009 vs 1.020 to three and four significant digits and calls a 1.004 at 72B 'near-lossless'. A paired bootstrap CI is mentioned exactly once (truncated) and never applied to the headline differences. NIAH cells are all multiples of 1/15 (100, 93.3, 86.7, 73.3, 46.7, 40.0), i.e. n=15 questions per cell -- so the entire 'KIVI degrades on retrieval' argument is a single question, and 'H2O degrades to 40-47%' is 6-7 questions. RULER sample sizes are never stated. Given that the field now expects matched-budget bootstrap audits (B ~ 50k paired records), 6 chunks and 15 needles is far below the current bar.

The 17-baseline suite is entirely self-reimplemented and at least one reimplementation is demonstrably broken, which undermines every comparative claim. SnapKV scores 27.1 on MMLU for Llama-2-7B against Full KV 47.3 -- below the 25% random-guess floor for 4-way MMLU. No published SnapKV result resembles this. The paper verifies only the H2O collapse (via a per-head reimplementation) and never audits SnapKV. The abstract's most dramatic number, 'H2O at 4x collapses (83x PPL)' at 32K, is likewise from an unaudited reimplementation at a context length where the published H2O configuration is not validated. The two closest competitors (MoE-nD, xKV) are also authors' reimplementations, and both conveniently lose. Please run against a public harness (e.g. NVIDIA KVPress, which already exposes per-layer compression and quantized-cache support and a public leaderboard) or against official artifacts.

Missing baselines and dated benchmarks relative to the 2026 state of the field. Directly overlapping work that is neither compared against nor argued away: RDKV (rate-distortion joint eviction+quantization bit allocation, training-free, TriZone packed-decode kernel, 97.81% of full-cache accuracy at 2.48% retention), HqeKV (ACL 2026 Findings, hybrid quantization+eviction, public code), PolyKV (layer-wise heterogeneous retention+allocation), ARKV (per-layer original/quant ratios from prefill statistics). Top-venue 2026 results setting the bar -- STAR-KV (ICML 2026 Spotlight, 20x with mixed-precision), KVTC (ICLR 2026, 20-40x), Layer-DefensiveKV (ICLR 2026, RULER 91.4 at 20% cache), TurboQuant (ICLR 2026) -- are absent. On benchmarks: the paper's primary metric is WikiText-2 PPL; it uses LongBench-v1 (now considered dated) and reports scores of 0.056/0.040/0.050 mean F1/ROUGE-L, which are two to three orders of magnitude below normal LongBench scores and include H2O 'beating' Full KV (0.097 vs 0.050) -- that table is evidence of a broken harness, not of quality. LongBench-v2, InfiniteBench, SCBench, and RULER beyond a single 72B/4096 column are all omitted.

The quality model Q = C*F*w is load-bearing but unjustified, and its own arithmetic contradicts the paper's flagship design principle. (i) The paper claims 'at low CR, dQ/dM for a bit-upgrade exceeds that of a token-add at almost every layer'. Working the model at n=32, S=1024, g=0.5, b=4: token-add of 8 gives dQ = F(4)*[(40/1024)^0.5 - (32/1024)^0.5] = 0.9794*0.0208 = 0.0204 at dM = 0.25*M0, i.e. 0.0815/M0; bit-upgrade 4->8 gives dQ = C*(F(8)-F(4)) = 0.1768*0.0204 = 0.0036 at dM = 1.0*M0, i.e. 0.0036/M0. Token-add is ~22x better per byte, and the general condition for a bit-upgrade to win is dF/F > (1-g), i.e. g > 0.979, above the paper's entire reported Gini range (0.43-0.93). Under the stated model, bit-upgrades are never chosen first. (ii) The Theoretical Properties section states dF_{4->8} = 0.0035, but the per-model calibration table gives 0.9998-0.9794 = 0.0204 for Mistral (mean ~0.024) -- a 6x discrepancy in a constant used to argue diminishing returns. (iii) The claim 'greedy achieves 118-119%' is stated against an unnamed referent; if that referent is the MCKP optimum of the same objective, a value above 100% is impossible for a maximization problem. (iv) The paper never shows that maximizing sum Q correlates with lower PPL on any model; only C is validated, on one model.

The motivating numbers do not survive checking. The introduction states 'At FP16, Llama-2-70B at 8K context requires over 40 GB', but the paper's own formula gives 2*80*8192*8*128*2 bytes = 2.68 GB for Llama-2-70B (80 layers, 8 GQA KV heads, d=128) -- wrong by ~16x, and even an MHA 64-head variant would be 21.5 GB. Separately, the two profiling analyses that motivate the whole method -- the Gini spread 0.43-0.93 ('a 2.1x spread', a meaningless ratio for a bounded index) and the rho = 0.194 correlation that supposedly proves the signals are 'complementary' -- are both measured on TinyLlama-1.1B, a model that appears in no results table, and both figures (allocation heatmap, signal curves) are TinyLlama-only. A weak correlation is equally consistent with one signal being noise; the paper offers no evidence that the Gini signal adds anything, and its own budget sweep says Gini has no effect below 3.5x.

The claimed differentiator versus the closest concurrent work evaporates in the deployment recipe. Appendix B's positioning table marks MoE-nD 'offline' and LayerBudget 'Online (check)', and the Related Work paragraph rests the distinction on 'online marginal-gain solver' vs their 'offline-calibrated greedy solver'. But the profiling-overhead table states that 'For deployment, fixed profiles (calibrated once per model) reduce the per-input overhead to <3%', and the ablation recommends 'a per-architecture LOO probe (5 prompts) ... is the recommended deployment recipe'. Both of those are offline calibration. If the recommended configuration is offline-profiled, the sole claimed axis of novelty against MoE-nD is gone and the positioning table's Online column is wrong.

System-level results are negative and presented as if they were not. The memory-savings table's footnote concedes 'Speedup <1x due to compression overhead'; decode latency is +2.6% to +12.2% TPOT; the vLLM integration is evaluated at 512 tokens; and the profiling pipeline adds 61-109% overhead (Limitation 2). For a paper whose entire premise is inference efficiency, there is no configuration in which it is measurably faster than the baseline, and the claimed memory savings do not match the nominal CR (24.3% at nominal 2x on Llama-2-7B).

Presentation and submission-format defects that are desk-reject risks. The source as submitted does not compile: '\begin{table[t]' (missing brace, importance-ablation table), '\section{Analysis' (unclosed brace), '\textbf{Downstream accuracy.' (unclosed brace), an unclosed parenthesis in 'On LongBench (16 English tasks, Table~[REF]', and four displayed equations with no math environment. Table 2 is wrapped in '\resizebox{\textwidth}{!}' over 18 columns plus '\tabcolsep 2pt', which reduces the effective font well below the template size -- the CFP explicitly lists decreased font sizes as a desk-reject trigger -- and there are repeated negative '\vspace' hacks. Numerous sentences terminate mid-number ('by 96\', 'retains 100\', '118--119\'), consistent with unescaped '%' swallowing the remainder of the line, which would leave truncated claims in the compiled PDF. There is no '\section{Limitations}' header; the limitations text is orphaned inside the malformed Analysis block. Finally, the submission contains three promises to fix known defects at camera-ready ('we will update against their official code at camera-ready'; 'For the camera-ready we will regenerate Table [REF]') -- a submission must be judged on what it contains, and conceding a known accounting error with a promise is not a fix.

The 'inverted importance' contribution is billed as a discovery but is shown by the authors' own probe to be a single-model artifact, and its effect at the headline operating point is within noise. Contribution 2 claims early layers are 'the primary quality bottleneck under eviction -- reversing the conventional assumption'. The paper then reports that Llama-2-13B is late-bottleneck (+0.093 late vs +0.030 early) and Qwen2.5-14B is flat (+0.039 vs +0.038): the finding holds on 1 of 3 models probed. Meanwhile the importance ablation at 4x -- the CR the abstract headlines -- shows Inverted 1.008 vs Flat 1.010 on Mistral and 1.002 vs 1.067 on Llama-2, i.e. a 0.002 difference on the model the prior was tuned on. The 60-94% improvement figures are all at 6x under zero-fill, a regime where the absolute quality (2.52, 1.283) is unusable anyway. Also, Eq. (importance) as written, sigma(k*(1 - l/(L-1) - tau)), is already monotonically decreasing in l -- i.e. it IS the early-high scheme -- yet the ablation table lists 'Sigmoid (late-high)' as a distinct scheme whose formula is never given.
questions: In Table 2 and Table 1, were the eviction baselines (H2O, SnapKV, StreamingLLM, MiniKV) evaluated with mean-fill, or with zero-fill? Your own data shows fill mode changes Llama-2-7B at 6x by a factor of 40 (45.09 -> 1.13), which is the same order as the abstract's 'H2O collapses to 83x' headline. If the baselines were zero-filled while LayerBudget was mean-filled, please rerun all comparative tables with fill mode matched and report the corrected numbers.

Please point to the memory-matched comparison table that the abstract ('ranks first ... at memory-matched comparison') and Section 'CR definition' ('we report a memory-matched comparison in Appendix [REF]') both cite. I could not find it in the submission. Absent that table, what is the evidence that LayerBudget beats uniform INT4 (KIVI) at equal bytes on any metric and any model?

The memory-savings table reports Llama-3.1-8B base KV as 189 MB and Mistral-7B as 95 MB at S=512, but the two models have identical KV geometry (32 layers, 8 KV heads, d=128); your own formula gives ~67 MB for both. It also reports 24.3% savings at nominal CR=2x on Llama-2-7B, an effective CR of 1.32, while the Byte-CR appendix asserts every method matches its nominal CR within +/-0.05. Which of these three numbers is correct, and can you republish all memory numbers under one accounting?

Your component ablation (A1) shows quant-only at 1.00/1.01 versus joint at 3.23/45.09 at 6x, and the budget sweep shows all signal variants tied below 3.5x. Is there any (model, CR, metric) triple with adequate statistical power where the per-layer joint allocator beats uniform INT4 at matched bytes? If so, please give the table; if not, why is joint allocation the primary contribution rather than mean-fill?

How many questions are in each NIAH cell and each RULER cell? The NIAH values are all multiples of 1/15, which would make the 'KIVI drops to 93.3%' claim a one-question difference and the sole empirical basis for preferring LayerBudget over KIVI. Please report per-cell n and confidence intervals, and add a long-context (16K/32K) retrieval evaluation -- currently the 32K claims are PPL-only, which by your own KIVI argument is the metric that cannot detect retrieval failure.

Section 3.5 argues 'dQ/dM for a bit-upgrade exceeds that of a token-add at almost every layer', but the model implies a bit-upgrade wins only when dF/F > (1-g), i.e. g > 0.979, which is outside your reported Gini range 0.43-0.93 (worked example at n=32, S=1024, g=0.5: token-add 0.0815/M0 vs bit-upgrade 0.0036/M0). Does the implementation use the Q of Eq. (2)-(4), or an additional term not described? Relatedly, why does Section 3.5 state dF_{4->8} = 0.0035 when the calibration table gives 0.0204 for Mistral?

What is the referent of '118-119%'? If it is the MCKP optimum of your own objective, a greedy heuristic cannot exceed 100% on a maximization problem; if it is a uniform-allocation baseline, please say so and give the baseline's definition.

SnapKV scores 27.1 on MMLU for Llama-2-7B, below the 25% random-guess floor, and LongBench overall scores are 0.040-0.097 where published values are one to two orders of magnitude higher, with H2O exceeding Full KV. Have these two harnesses been validated against any published reference number? Would you be willing to rerun the baseline suite inside a public harness (e.g. KVPress) so the 17-baseline claim can be checked independently?

If the recommended deployment recipe uses fixed per-model profiles and a per-architecture LOO probe (both offline calibration), on what basis is LayerBudget marked 'Online' and MoE-nD 'offline' in the Appendix B positioning table, which is the paper's stated axis of novelty against the closest concurrent work?

probe_answers.answer: Alternatives that plausibly solve the same problem. (1) KIVI / uniform INT4 quantization -- compared head-to-head, and it WINS or ties on the headline metric at 4x and 6x on all seven models (Table 2, Table 1, large-model table, 72B table) and in the memory-vs-quality table uses less memory (9,990 KB vs 12,939 KB) at better PPL (1.01 vs 1.07). The paper does not argue it is insufficient; it redefines the ranking category ('first among token-compression methods') to exclude it, and rests the remaining argument on NIAH cells of n=15 where KIVI ties on 6 of 7 models. (2) RDKV (rate-distortion bit allocation for joint eviction+quantization, training-free, reverse water-filling, TriZone packed-decode kernel; 97.81% of full-cache accuracy at 2.48% retention, 4.5x decode speedup at 128K) -- IGNORED ENTIRELY. This is the same formulation with a principled derivation, a real kernel, and speedups the paper cannot show. (3) HqeKV (ACL 2026 Findings, hybrid quantization+eviction with an integrated per-element optimizer and joint K-V importance, code public) -- IGNORED ENTIRELY, despite being published, directly overlapping, and reproducible. (4) PolyKV (layer-wise coupling of eviction pattern and capacity under a shared memory constraint) and ARKV (per-layer original/quant ratios from prefill attention statistics) -- IGNORED. (5) STAR-KV (ICML 2026 Spotlight; low-rank + mixed-precision, 20x, 6.9x faster attention) and KVTC (ICLR 2026; PCA + adaptive quantization + entropy coding under a global bit budget, 20-40x) -- IGNORED; both operate at compression ratios 3-5x beyond this paper's usable envelope. (6) Layer-DefensiveKV (ICLR 2026; layer-wise budget allocation, RULER 91.4 at 20% cache) -- IGNORED, and it is the closest published per-layer-allocation result. (7) NVIDIA KVPress, the de-facto harness with built-in PerLayerCompressionPress and QuantizedCache -- not used; the paper reimplements 17 baselines itself instead. Only MoE-nD and xKV are addressed head-to-head, and both are the authors' own reimplementations. Ignoring RDKV, HqeKV, and the ICLR/ICML 2026 line while claiming 'to our knowledge, no prior online, training-free method jointly optimizes per-layer (n_l, b_l)' is a fatal weakness of the related-work positioning.

Cold, overloaded, or undefined terms. (1) 'CR' is overloaded five ways: nominal CR, token-count CR, method-byte CR, allocator-side CR, and pipeline-measured effective CR (Section 'CR definition' + Byte-CR Reconciliation appendix). Tables never state which one a column uses, and the two differ by 2x on the paper's own admission. (2) 'Sigmoid' is overloaded: Eq. (4) sigma(k*(1 - l/(L-1) - tau)) is monotonically DECREASING in l, i.e. early-high, and the text says so ('This default assigns higher weight to early layers'), yet the ablation table lists 'Sigmoid (late-high)' as a distinct scheme whose formula is never given. Two different objects, one name. (3) Q(l, n_l, b_l) -- called a 'quality model' but its units, range, and relation to any measurable quality (PPL, accuracy) are never stated; sum_l Q is maximized without ever being shown to track anything. (4) '118-119%' -- percent OF WHAT is never stated (the sentence is truncated in the submitted text); if of the MCKP optimum, >100% is impossible. (5) n_min = 'sink + recent' -- the sink count and recent-window size are never given numerically anywhere in the paper or the algorithm box. (6) B_used appears in the algorithm box (line 2 of the WHILE) but is never defined. (7) 'Ph', 'Qt', 'Jt', 'Evict' category labels in Table 2 and 'LB' in the NIAH tables are never expanded. (8) 'Gini stability finding from Section [REF]' is referenced in the long-context section, but no Gini-stability analysis appears anywhere in the paper -- a dangling reference to a nonexistent result. (9) 'memory-matched comparison (Appendix [REF])' -- cited twice, does not exist. (10) 'g_l' -- whether the Gini is recomputed per input (the 'online' claim) or from a fixed per-model profile (the 'deployment' recipe) is left ambiguous, and the two imply different methods.

Four recomputations, three of which fail. (A) Motivating KV size. Intro: 'At FP16, Llama-2-70B at 8K context requires over 40 GB'. Using the paper's OWN formula 2*L*S*H*d*b bytes with L=80, S=8192, H=8 (Llama-2-70B is GQA with 8 KV heads), d=128, b=2 bytes: 2*80*8192*8*128*2 = 2,684,354,560 bytes = 2.68 GB (2.5 GiB). The claim is wrong by ~16x; even a hypothetical 64-head MHA variant gives 21.5 GB, still short of 40. FAILS. (B) Greedy action ordering vs the 'quantize first' principle. At the allocator's initial state (n=n_min~32, S=1024, g=0.5, b=4), C = (32/1024)^0.5 = 0.1768. Token-add (dn=8): C' = (40/1024)^0.5 = 0.1976, dQ = F(4)*dC = 0.9794*0.0208 = 0.02037, dM = M0*(8/32) = 0.25*M0, so dQ/dM = 0.0815/M0. Bit-upgrade 4->8: dQ = C*(F(8)-F(4)) = 0.1768*(0.9998-0.9794) = 0.003607, dM = M0 (bytes double), so dQ/dM = 0.0036/M0. Token-add is 22.6x better per byte. Generally, a bit-upgrade wins only if dF/F > (1-g), i.e. 0.0208 > (1-g), i.e. g > 0.979 -- above the entire reported Gini range 0.43-0.93. The Theoretical Properties claim that bit-upgrades dominate 'at almost every layer' is therefore contradicted by the paper's own equations and calibration constants. FAILS. (C) Fidelity constant. Section 3.5 states dF_{4->8} = 0.0035; the per-model calibration table gives 0.9998 - 0.9794 = 0.0204 (Mistral), mean over the six models 1.000-0.976 = 0.024. Off by ~6x. FAILS. (D) Allocator latency. The paper computes 80*32768/8 = 327,680 iterations and 327,680 * 30 ns = 9.8 ms ~ '10 ms' -- that arithmetic is right, but the cost model is not: each WHILE iteration must scan all L layers x 2 actions to take the argmax, so total comparisons are L^2*S/dn = 80*327,680 = 26.2M, giving 26.2e6 * 30 ns = 786 ms, ~80x the projected figure and far from 'small relative to a single decode step'. The stated O(L*S/dn) counts applied actions, not work. FAILS as stated. (E) One check that PASSES: the KL reductions, 0.249 -> 0.009 = 96.4% and 0.6696 -> 0.0636 = 90.5%, are arithmetically correct.

Yes, and the most favorable abstract numbers are not the honest ones. (1) 'At 32K context on Mistral-7B, H2O at 4x collapses (83x PPL)' is the abstract's most quotable number. It comes from an authors' reimplementation of H2O, at a context length where the reimplementation is never validated against any published reference; the only H2O audit performed in the paper is for MMLU at short context. Moreover the paper's own data shows that fill mode alone moves a 6x Llama-2-7B result from 45.09 to 1.13 -- so if LayerBudget was mean-filled and H2O zero-filled in that table, the 83x is a fill-mode artifact. (2) SnapKV at 27.1 MMLU on Llama-2-7B is below the 25% chance floor; a baseline performing below random is misconfigured, and it appears in the paper as evidence that competitors collapse. (3) LongBench scores of 0.040-0.097 across all methods including Full KV are two orders of magnitude below normal LongBench values, and H2O 'beats' Full KV by 2x on Llama-2-7B (0.097 vs 0.050), explained away in a footnote. That table cannot support any claim. (4) The two closest competitors, MoE-nD and xKV, are both the authors' reimplementations ('the official artifacts were not public at submission time') and both lose. (5) Honest-number audit of the abstract: '<=1.03 at 4x on seven models' is false (Llama-2-13B = 1.11); 'ranks first among token-compression methods ... at memory-matched comparison' has no supporting table and is contradicted by the one memory table that exists (KIVI 9,990 KB/1.01 vs LB 12,939 KB/1.07); 'NIAH retains 100%' is contradicted for Mistral-7B (73.3 at 4x, versus Full KV 86.7). The honest headline would be: 'matches uniform INT4 quantization at 2-4x, loses to it at 6x, and adds token-count reduction at the cost of 3-12% decode latency and no measured speedup.'

Ten internal contradictions. (1) Intro '>40 GB' for Llama-2-70B 8K FP16 vs the paper's own memory formula giving 2.68 GB. (2) Section 3.5's dF_{4->8} = 0.0035 vs the calibration table's 0.0204. (3) Byte-CR appendix: 'every method's effective CR matches its nominal CR within +/-0.05' vs the memory-savings table's 24.3% savings at nominal 2x (effective 1.32) and 71.2% (effective 3.47). (4) Llama-3.1-8B base KV 189 MB vs Mistral-7B 95 MB at S=512 despite identical KV geometry; neither matches the paper's own formula (~67 MB). (5) 'Under zero-fill evaluation (the practical deployment setting)' vs every headline table being mean-fill. (6) Abstract 'ranks first ... at memory-matched comparison' vs no memory-matched table, and vs the 6x memory table where LB uses more memory at worse PPL than KIVI. (7) Abstract '<=1.03 at 4x on seven models' vs Llama-2-13B at 1.11. (8) 'LayerBudget matches Full KV accuracy on every model (100%)' at 4x NIAH vs Mistral-7B LB = 73.3 (Full KV 86.7). (9) 'ranks 1st among all token-compression methods at every configuration across all four models' vs MiniKV 1.07 < LB 1.08 on Llama-3.1-8B at 6x. (10) Appendix B marks LayerBudget 'Online' as its differentiator vs MoE-nD's 'offline', while the profiling table and the ablation both recommend offline fixed profiles and an offline per-architecture LOO probe as the deployment recipe. (11) Section 3.5 asserts bit-upgrades dominate token-adds per byte; Eq. (2)-(4) with the paper's constants say the opposite by ~22x. (12) Contribution 5 claims '<=1.009' at 16K-32K vs Llama-3.1-8B at 1.035.

The prose shows strong machine-generated / rebuttal-pasted signatures. (a) 'Not X but Y' and defensive-negation parallelism appears at least five times, always immediately after an inconvenient number: 'the value is the measured ratio (not a typo)' (Table 2 footnote); 'so the flat ~1.03 PPL across moderate CR is not solver degeneracy' (LB-KV appendix); 'the 2x inflation in the table below is allocator overhead, not a CR-denominator inconsistency between methods'; 'not the 3.0x that Table [REF]'s allocator-side numbers would imply'; 'We therefore treat inverted importance as a Mistral-tuned default, not a universal principle'. (b) Captions argue instead of describing: the Table 1 caption is five sentences of advocacy ('LayerBudget (shared b_l) wins at moderate CR ... trailing MoE-nD by only 2pp ... while improving over LayerBudget by 19pp'), and the A1 caption is a seven-line defense of a result that contradicts the paper. (c) Reviewer-response text is embedded verbatim in the submission: 'we will update against their official code at camera-ready'; 'For the camera-ready we will regenerate Table [REF] using mean_memory_bytes as the denominator'; 'Caveat on baselines:' introducing a 200-word paragraph inside Related Work. These read as replies to a prior report, not as authored exposition. (d) Uniform rhythm of 'claim + hedge + forward-promise' in the Related Work MoE-nD paragraph, which is a single ~400-word block that concedes a loss, introduces an unlisted second method to cover it, and concludes with the framing sentence 'The two design points are therefore best read as complementary operating regimes of the same framework rather than two competing solvers' -- an assertion with no supporting evidence, phrased to neutralize a negative result. (e) Section 'Analysis' has no topic sentence and no section-level argument; it opens mid-stream at 'Mean-fill preserves attention structure' and runs into the limitations list without a header.

(a) OVER-ASSERTION. 'Nearly all existing methods apply their strategy uniformly across layers' -- contradicted one paragraph later by PyramidKV, D2O, SqueezeAttention, CAKE, Ada-KV, EvolKV, LAVa, all of which the paper itself describes as per-layer or per-head. 'LayerBudget ranks 1st among all token-compression methods. At every configuration across all four models' -- falsified by MiniKV at Llama-3.1-8B 6x. 'attention sparsity profiles calibrated at short context transfer to 32K tokens without recalibration' -- stated as established, evidenced only by PPL, and attributed to a 'Gini stability finding' that does not exist in the paper. 'To our knowledge, no prior online, training-free method jointly optimizes per-layer (n_l, b_l) across the model architectures and operating regimes we evaluate' -- the trailing clause makes the claim unfalsifiable. 'KV cache compression is most impactful at long context' -- asserted, never measured (no long-context task metric is reported). (b) VAGUE REFERENT. 'This weak correlation means the two signals provide complementary information' -- 'complementary' does not follow from rho = 0.194; the same evidence supports 'one signal is uninformative'. 'The reduction generalizes' (mean-fill) -- from n=2 models. 'We address this regime with an independent-bits variant' -- 'this regime' could be CR=6x, Mistral specifically, or extreme CR generally; the variant's NIAH then collapses to 26.7%. 'the relative ordering of methods at any fixed CR is unchanged by this rederivation' -- 'this rederivation' has not been performed. (c) THING-VS-PROCESS. 'allocation' denotes both the greedy procedure and the (n_l, b_l) plan it outputs ('the allocation differs at every CR' vs 'per-layer joint allocation'); 'profiling' denotes both the pipeline and its latency ('the full profiling pipeline adds 61-109%' vs 'fixed profiles'); 'importance' denotes both the hand-set sigmoid weights w_l and the LOO-measured empirical sensitivity, which are the objects the paper is trying to distinguish; 'compression' denotes both the target CR and the achieved byte reduction, which the memory table shows differ by up to 1.5x. (d) FALSE PRECISION. 'PPL ratio 1.004 at 4x' at 72B and '1.009x' at 32K, reported to four digits from 6 chunks whose stated cross-chunk std is ~2.3. 'reduces output KL divergence by 96%' from one (model, CR) point. 'improve 6x compression by 60-94%' -- a percentage change of a PPL ratio whose floor is 1.0. 'MAE 3.1%' on one model. 'F(8) is consistent at 0.9997-0.9999' -- four decimals over 8 calibration prompts. '-0.6%' and '-2.2%' prefill 'overhead' -- negative overheads are noise reported as measurements. 'Gini ... a 2.1x spread' -- a ratio of two Gini coefficients is not a meaningful quantity.

Thesis in one sentence: 'Allocating token-retention count and KV bit-width jointly and per-layer, spending quantization headroom before evicting, yields near-lossless KV cache compression at 2-4x across 7B-72B models.' Topic sentences and mapping: Intro P1 (KV cache is the memory bottleneck) -> maps, but its evidence (the 40 GB figure) is wrong by 16x, so evidence does not map to its own topic sentence. Intro P2 (two families exist) -> maps. Intro P3 ('The uniform assumption') -> claims uniformity is near-universal; its own Related Work refutes this, so evidence contradicts the topic sentence. Intro P4 ('Our insight: quantize first, evict last') -> maps to thesis, but the mechanism it asserts is contradicted by the paper's own equations (P3-B). Related Work P1-P3 -> map. Related Work P4 (MoE-nD, ~400 words) -> does not map to the thesis: it is a defense of a loss plus the introduction of a second method (LayerBudget-KV) that appears in no contribution list; it argues rather than positions. Method 3.1-3.4 -> map. Method 3.5 (Theoretical Properties) -> topic sentence claims MCKP structure, then disclaims every guarantee ('We do not claim the standard (1-1/e) bound'; 'an FPTAS exists but is impractical'); the paragraph establishes nothing and is a deletion candidate as written. Experiments 'Key findings' bullet 6 ('GQA models are more robust ... GQA models also achieve higher memory savings 43-72%') -> maps to NEITHER the thesis nor its own topic sentence: it is a claim about model architectures, the mechanism ('shared KV heads provide natural redundancy') is asserted with no experiment, and the memory-savings half is a property of the base model, not of the method -- and it rests on the two numbers that are internally inconsistent (189 vs 95 MB). Long-Context section -> maps, but contains zero in-body tables. End-to-End Validation -> maps partially; the vLLM paragraph reports a single 512-token result and no throughput. 'Analysis' section -> I cannot identify a topic sentence; it opens at 'Mean-fill preserves attention structure' and merges into an unlabelled limitations list. That is itself the finding. Byte-CR Reconciliation appendix -> maps to neither: it explains why a discrepancy should be tolerated and promises to fix it later; it presents no new evidence. LayerBudget-KV appendix -> introduces an unlisted second method whose retrieval collapses to 26.7%; it maps to the rebuttal, not the thesis.

I have only the LaTeX source; ppl_scaling.pdf, allocation_heatmap.pdf, and signal_curves.pdf were not provided, so I could not inspect any figure as rendered. I flag that the figures are UNVERIFIABLE and that this alone prevents me from certifying the paper's visual claims. From the captions and text I can nonetheless note three defects. (1) Two of the three figures (allocation heatmap, signal curves) are on TinyLlama-1.1B, a model that appears in no results table and is not in the seven-model suite -- so the only visualizations of the method's core mechanism are on a model whose results are never reported. (2) Figure 1's caption states LayerBudget 'matches KIVI at 2-3x', which is an admission that the figure shows no advantage over the baseline at the CRs the abstract headlines; and 'GQA models (solid) are more robust than MHA (dashed)' is a claim about model architecture, not about the method. (3) A systems/method paper with three figures and no diagram of the allocator, the action space, or the mean-fill mechanism is under-illustrated; the algorithm is conveyed only by a 9-line pseudocode box that omits the definitions of n_min, sink, recent, and B_used. Additionally, Table 2 is wrapped in \resizebox{\textwidth}{!} over 18 columns, which will render at a font size well below the template's -- a rendering defect and a format-policy risk (see P10).

(a) ANONYMITY: no author, institution, funding, or repository leak found; 'the official artifacts were not public at submission time' and 'we will update ... at camera-ready' do not de-anonymize. However, three forward-promises to fix known defects at camera-ready ('we will update against their official code at camera-ready'; 'For the camera-ready we will regenerate Table [REF] using mean_memory_bytes as the denominator') are improper in a submission: they concede that a reported table uses an accounting the authors already know is wrong, and ask reviewers to score the promised version. No aggressive priority claim beyond the standard 'to our knowledge' sentence, which is hedged into vacuity. (b) COMPLETENESS: \input{checklist} is present, so the checklist file is included, but its contents are not in the text I was given -- I cannot verify that the NeurIPS LLM-usage item, the limitations item, or the compute/reproducibility items are answered. FLAGGED AS UNVERIFIED. Separately, there is no \section{Limitations}: the limitations list is orphaned inside a malformed '\section{Analysis' block, which the checklist's limitations item normally has to point at. (c) FORMAT: the source as submitted will not compile -- '\begin{table[t]' (missing closing brace on the environment name, importance-ablation table), '\section{Analysis' (unclosed brace), '\textbf{Downstream accuracy.' (unclosed brace), an unclosed parenthesis in 'On LongBench (16 English tasks, Table~[REF]', and four displayed equations (problem formulation, Q decomposition, coverage law, importance) written without any math environment. A submission that does not build is a desk-reject risk on its own. Font/margin policy: Table 2 uses \resizebox{\textwidth}{!} across 18 columns together with \tabcolsep=2pt, and several \vspace{-0.2in}/-0.1in/-0.05in hacks appear around figures and tables; the CFP states that submissions 'violating the NeurIPS style (e.g., by decreasing margins or font sizes) ... may be desk rejected', and a full-width resizebox on an 18-column table is exactly a font-size reduction. Page count could not be verified without a PDF, though the main body (7 sections, 3 tables, 3 figures) plausibly fits nine pages -- in part because nearly all evidence has been pushed into the appendix, which is itself a presentation problem since reviewers are not obliged to read it. Finally, numerous sentences terminate mid-number ('by 96\', 'retains 100\', '118--119\', '60\', 'PPL ratio $\leq$1.002 at 2--4$\times$, with 33.7\'), consistent with unescaped '%' characters commenting out the rest of the line; in the compiled PDF these would appear as truncated claims, including in the abstract.

Theory-to-implementation coherence fails in three places. (a) What the algorithm actually computes: the algorithm box maximizes sum_l Q(l, n_l, b_l) = C(l,n_l) * F(b_l) * w_l subject to sum_l M(n_l,b_l) <= B, by greedily applying the (layer, action) with maximal dQ/dM. (b) Does that equal the object the theory names? No. The theory names 'quality', and the paper's evaluation metric is PPL ratio / task accuracy, but nowhere is sum Q shown to correlate with either. C is validated once (attention-mass MAE 3.1%, Mistral only); F is a cosine similarity between full and dequantized tensors, used multiplicatively as if quality were linear in cosine fidelity, with no justification; w_l is a hand-set sigmoid with hyperparameters k=5, tau=0.3 chosen without any stated procedure. A product of one validated proxy, one unjustified proxy, and one hand-set prior is asserted to be the thing worth maximizing. (c) Semantics silently changed. First, the paper's flagship design principle ('quantize first, evict last') is claimed to 'emerge naturally from the marginal gains ... dQ/dM for a bit-upgrade exceeds that of a token-add at almost every layer'. Under the paper's own equations and calibration constants, a bit-upgrade wins only when dF/F > (1-g), i.e. g > 0.979, which is above the entire reported Gini range 0.43-0.93; at n=32, S=1024, g=0.5 the token-add is 22.6x better per byte (worked in P3). So the stated mechanism is not what the described allocator does. The observed 'no eviction below 3.5x' behaviour follows trivially from the byte budget -- INT4 alone buys exactly 4x, so any CR <= 4x is satisfiable with zero eviction regardless of allocation -- which the paper itself concedes ('At 1.5-3.5x: all signal variants are equivalent ... Gini has no effect'). The per-layer machinery is therefore inert in precisely the regime where the paper reports near-lossless results. Second, Eq. (4) as written is monotonically decreasing in l (early-high), which is the scheme the paper calls 'Inverted', yet the ablation table lists 'Sigmoid (late-high)' as a different scheme with no formula -- the equation in the method section does not correspond to the baseline it is ablated against. Third, the theory section claims MCKP structure and then disclaims every guarantee, so the '118-119%' figure is the only quantitative claim about solution quality, and its referent is undefined (if it is the MCKP optimum, exceeding 100% is impossible). A method whose stated mechanism contradicts its own equations, and whose objective is never tied to the reported metric, is not a proved-and-run system.

Contributions in the order claimed, each with its isolating experiment and measured marginal effect. C1, per-layer joint (n_l,b_l) greedy allocation with calibrated fidelity constants ('118-119%'). Isolating experiments: component analysis A1 and precision ablation A3 and the budget sweep. Measured effect: at 3x, joint = quant-only = eviction-only (Mistral 1.00/1.00/1.00; Llama-2 1.02/1.02/1.00, where eviction-only WINS); at 6x, joint is worse than both parts (Mistral 3.23 vs 1.00 and 3.18; Llama-2 45.09 vs 1.01 and 44.71); A3 shows {4,16} and {4,8,16} identical at 3 of 4 cells; the budget sweep shows all variants tied at 1.5-3.5x with the explicit statement that 'Gini has no effect'. Marginal effect: ZERO in the near-lossless regime, NEGATIVE at 6x. FATAL. C2, inverted importance from LOO ('improves 6x compression by 60-94%'). Isolating experiment: importance-direction ablation. Effect at the headline 4x: Mistral 1.008 (inverted) vs 1.010 (flat) = 0.002, within the paper's own noise; Llama-2 1.002 vs 1.067. Large effect only at 6x under zero-fill where absolute quality is unusable (2.52), and the paper's own LOO re-runs show the direction reverses on Llama-2-13B and vanishes on Qwen2.5-14B, i.e. it holds on 1 of 3 models probed. C3, mean-fill. Isolating experiment: KL and PPL comparisons. Effect: the largest in the paper by an order of magnitude (KL 0.249->0.009; PPL 45.09->1.13, i.e. it accounts for ~97.5% of the Llama-2 6x improvement). But mean-fill is a generic fill rule available to every eviction baseline, and the paper does not state whether baselines received it. C4, controlled comparison of 17 baselines. No isolating experiment applies, but the suite is unvalidated (SnapKV below chance on MMLU; LongBench scores two orders of magnitude off). C5, 16K-32K validation. Reported, but PPL-only, and the claimed '<=1.009' is false for Llama-3.1-8B (1.035). C6, 72B scaling. Reported; LB 1.004 vs KIVI 1.000 at 4x, i.e. LB loses. Ranking by measured marginal effect: mean-fill >> inverted importance (model-specific, ~0.002 at 4x) >> joint allocation (0 or negative). The abstract's implied ranking is exactly the reverse: joint allocation is billed as the method, mean-fill as a minor addition. A primary contribution whose isolating experiment shows a negative effect is a fatal credit-assignment defect; the honest fix is to demote the allocator and reframe the paper around mean-fill -- with baselines given mean-fill too.

(a) One-sentence contribution in this community's vocabulary: 'A training-free, per-layer joint allocation of KV-cache token budget and quantization bit-width, solved greedily against an attention-sparsity coverage model, plus a mean-imputation rule for evicted KV entries.' That sentence is expressible, so the paper is not mis-venued in topic -- efficient LLM inference and KV-cache compression are squarely within NeurIPS/ICLR/MLSys scope. (b) Terms a PC member would have to look up or would not use: 'coverage law' (not standard; it is an assumed power-law fit), 'fidelity constant F(b)' (cosine similarity repurposed as a quality multiplier), 'mean-fill' (the authors' coinage for mean imputation of evicted KV), 'the MoE-nD framing' (used as a method name for the authors' own reimplementation), 'inverted importance', 'byte-CR reconciliation'. None are fatal, but four of six are the paper's own coinages used as if established. (c) No core mechanism belongs to a different community. The mis-fit is one of depth rather than field: the ML side offers a hand-set heuristic with no guarantee and an objective never tied to the reported metric, while the systems side reports no speedup (the paper's own footnote says 'Speedup <1x'), +3-12% TPOT, a 512-token vLLM demo, and no kernel -- so it is under-strength for MLSys/ASPLOS on the systems axis and under-strength for NeurIPS/ICLR on the methodological axis. (d) Related work positions against a preprint slice (arXiv 2024-2026: H2O, SnapKV, PyramidKV, D2O, CAKE, Ada-KV, EvolKV, LAVa, KIVI, KVTuner, MiniKV, MoE-nD, xKV, EVICPRESS, KV Pareto, HCAttention, PoD) and misses the venue's own recent published literature in exactly this area: STAR-KV (ICML 2026 Spotlight), KVTC (ICLR 2026), DefensiveKV / Layer-DefensiveKV (ICLR 2026), TurboQuant (ICLR 2026), 'Adaptive KV-Cache Compression without Manually Setting Budget' (ICLR 2026), HqeKV (ACL 2026 Findings). It also uses WikiText-2 PPL as the primary metric and LongBench-v1 rather than the benchmarks this community now expects (LongBench-v2, RULER at 4K-128K, InfiniteBench, SCBench), and does not report effective bits/token, the common currency in the 2026 literature. This is a real venue-fit defect: the paper argues against a 2024-vintage baseline set at 2-6x while the venue's accepted 2026 papers are reporting 20-40x.

(a) Metrics a reader expects for KV-cache compression in 2026, marked: WikiText-2 PPL REPORTED (primary); LongBench-v2 OMITTED; LongBench-v1 REPORTED but with scores of 0.040-0.097 that are two orders of magnitude below published values and in which H2O beats Full KV -- effectively unusable; RULER REPORTED only for Qwen2.5-72B at 4096, OMITTED for all six other models and for all lengths above 4K; InfiniteBench OMITTED; SCBench OMITTED; NIAH REPORTED but only at 4096 tokens with n=15 per cell; MMLU REPORTED; GSM8K REPORTED at n=200; AIME/MATH-500/LiveCodeBench (the reasoning-model regime) OMITTED; effective bits per token OMITTED; decode throughput / tokens-per-second OMITTED (only TPOT, which shows a 2.6-12.2% regression); peak memory at long context OMITTED (memory table stops at 4096); prefill latency REPORTED. (b) Do headline claims depend on omitted metrics? Yes, decisively. The headline 'remains near-lossless at 2x on 32K-token contexts' and 'H2O collapses at 32K' rest on PPL alone at 16K-32K, with no retrieval or task metric at those lengths. The paper's own KIVI argument establishes that PPL cannot detect retrieval failure (KIVI at PPL 1.01 but NIAH 93.3), so the one metric it reports at long context is the one it has itself declared insufficient. A 32K NIAH or RULER run could reverse the long-context claim; this is a fatal coverage gap. Likewise, the claim of superiority over KIVI depends entirely on NIAH at 4096 with n=15, where KIVI ties on 6 of 7 models. (c) Unmeasured terms in the paper's own objective: Q = C*F*w. The importance term w_l is never measured against anything -- there is no experiment relating w_l to any observed quantity (the LOO probe measures a different object and, on 2 of 3 models, contradicts w_l's shape). The product sum_l Q is never compared to PPL or accuracy, so the quantity being maximized is never shown to be the quantity that matters. The fidelity term F is measured (cosine similarity) but never validated as a predictor of downstream quality. (d) Workload regime vs claims: the claims are stated over 'long-context inference' and '7B-72B deployment', but the primary evidence is 1024-token WikiText-2 chunks on 4-bit-weight models, the vLLM integration is at 512 tokens, downstream tasks at 72B were skipped, NIAH stops at 4096, and no throughput or serving-level (batched) measurement appears anywhere. The evaluated regime does not match the regime the claims are stated over.
